The Solar System is centred on the Sun.
The Solar System is 4.6 billion years old.
The main components of the Solar System are the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, satellites, asteroids, comets, meteoroids and cosmic dust.
The current number of planets is eight.
The former number of planets was nine before Pluto’s reclassification.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the IAU.
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are terrestrial rocky planets.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are Jovian giant planets.
The inner planets in order are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
The outer planets in order are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Earth is third from the Sun.
Venus and Mars are Earth’s neighbours.
Mercury is the nearest planet to the Sun.
Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun.
Neptune has the longest revolution period at 165 years.
Earth is the densest planet, with a density of 5.5 g/cm³.
Jupiter has the highest gravitational acceleration.
Mercury is 57.9 million km from the Sun.
Venus is 108.2 million km from the Sun.
Earth is 149.6 million km from the Sun.
Mars is 228 million km from the Sun.
Jupiter is 778.5 million km from the Sun.
Saturn is 1,432 million km from the Sun.
Uranus is 2,867 million km from the Sun.
Neptune is 4,515 million km from the Sun.
Jupiter has a diameter of 142,984 km.
Saturn has a diameter of 120,536 km.
Uranus has a diameter of 51,118 km.
Neptune has a diameter of 49,528 km.
Earth has a diameter of 12,756 km.
Venus has a diameter of 12,104 km.
Mars has a diameter of 6,792 km.
Mercury has a diameter of 4,879 km.
Mercury revolves around the Sun in 88 days.
Venus revolves around the Sun in 224.7 days.
Earth revolves around the Sun in 365.25 days.
Mars revolves around the Sun in 687 days.
Jupiter revolves around the Sun in 11.86 years.
Saturn revolves around the Sun in 29.4 years.
Uranus revolves around the Sun in 84.07 years.
Neptune revolves around the Sun in 164.9 years.
Mercury has the fastest orbital velocity.
Neptune has the slowest orbital velocity.
Mercury and Venus have no natural satellites.
Venus is known as the Earth-twin.
Venus is known as the Morning and Evening Star.
Mars is known as the Red Planet.
Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.
The shape of Earth is a geoid or oblate spheroid.
Earth rotates from west to east.
Earth’s rotation produces day and night.
Earth revolves around the Sun in 365.25 days.
Earth’s revolution produces a year and seasons.
Earth’s mean distance from the Sun is 149.6 million km.
One astronomical unit is the mean Earth–Sun distance.
Sunlight takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach Earth.
The Sun is the closest star to Earth.
Earth’s habitable zone is called the Goldilocks Zone.
Earth is the only known life-supporting planet.
Rotation is the spinning of Earth on its axis.
Revolution is the movement of Earth around the Sun.
Earth’s revolution occurs around the Sun.
The direction of Earth’s revolution is around the Sun.
The daily cycle is associated with rotation.
Seasons are associated with revolution and axial tilt.
The Sun is overhead at the equator on 21 March.
Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere on 21 March.
Autumn begins in the Southern Hemisphere on 21 March.
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer on 21 June.
21 June is the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere.
21 June is winter in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Sun is overhead at the equator on 23 September.
Autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere on 23 September.
Spring begins in the Southern Hemisphere on 23 September.
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn on 22 December.
22 December is the winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere.
22 December is summer in the Southern Hemisphere.
The summer solstice occurs on 21 June.
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer during the summer solstice.
The winter solstice occurs on 22 December.
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn during the winter solstice.
The equinoxes occur on 21 March and 23 September.
Day and night are approximately equal during the equinoxes.
The Sun is a star at the centre of the Solar System.
The visible bright layer of the Sun is the photosphere.
The photosphere has a temperature of about 5,500°C.
The Sun’s core temperature is 15 million°C.
The interior of the Sun is in a plasma state.
The Sun’s energy comes from nuclear fusion.
Nuclear fusion in the Sun converts hydrogen into helium and releases energy.
The Sun contains 99.8% of the Solar System’s mass.
The Sun’s diameter is 109 times Earth’s diameter.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth.
A solar eclipse occurs during the new moon phase.
The corona is visible during a solar eclipse.
A sunspot is a dark patch on the photosphere.
An aurora is produced by solar particles interacting with the atmosphere.
Aurora Borealis occurs in the north.
Aurora Australis occurs in the south.
Perihelion is when Earth is closest to the Sun.
Earth reaches perihelion in early January.
Aphelion is when Earth is farthest from the Sun.
Earth reaches aphelion in early July.
An astronomical unit is the mean Earth–Sun distance.
One astronomical unit equals 149.6 million km.
One astronomical unit equals approximately 149.6 × 10⁹ m.
Light takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to travel one astronomical unit.
Orbital speed is higher at perihelion.
Orbital speed is lower at aphelion.
Earth is wider at the equator and flatter at the poles.
The centrifugal force is maximum at the equator.
An object’s weight is minimum at the equator.
An object’s weight is maximum at the poles.
Earth’s variation in weight is caused by rotation and its non-spherical shape.
The mantle lies below the crust.
The outer core consists of liquid iron and nickel.
The inner core consists of solid iron.
Earth’s core begins at a depth of 2,900 km.
NIFE means nickel and ferrum, or iron.
Aristotle was the first stated source for Earth’s spherical shape.
Aryabhatta explained the apparent daily motion of the Sun through Earth’s rotation.
The geomagnetic equator location was tested at Thumba.
Earth Day is observed on 22 April.
The first Earth Day was observed in 1970.
Alpha Centauri is the next closest star mentioned after the Sun.
The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite.
The Moon’s average distance from Earth is 384,400 km.
The Moon’s minimum distance from Earth is 363,300 km.
The Moon’s maximum distance from Earth is 405,500 km.
The Moon’s orbital and rotation period is 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes.
The Moon shows the same face toward Earth.
The Moon’s atmosphere is essentially absent.
The Moon’s gravity is one-sixth of Earth’s gravity.
A lunar eclipse occurs during the full moon phase.
Perigee is the Moon’s closest position to Earth.
Apogee is the Moon’s farthest position from Earth.
A supermoon is a full moon near perigee.
Apollo 11 made the first human landing on the Moon in 1969.
Apollo 11 landed in the Sea of Tranquility.
A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth is between the Sun and Moon.
During a solar eclipse, the Moon’s shadow falls on Earth.
During a lunar eclipse, Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.
A solar eclipse is visible from a limited region.
A lunar eclipse is visible over a larger part of the night side.
The corona is visible during a total solar eclipse.
The Moon may appear reddish during a lunar eclipse.
A full moon occurs when Earth is approximately between the Sun and Moon.
A new moon occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth.
A half moon occurs when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 90°.
A blue moon can mean two full moons in one calendar month.
At perigee, the Moon produces stronger gravity and higher tides.
A full moon at perigee is called a supermoon.
At apogee, the Moon produces weaker gravity.
The calendar definition of a blue moon is two full moons in one month.
The stated frequency of a blue moon is 2.7154 years.
A blue moon can alternatively mean an extra full moon in an astronomical season.
Asteroids are composed of rock and metal.
Comets are composed of ice, dust and rock.
The main asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
Comets occur in the outer system, including the Kuiper and Oort regions.
Asteroids generally do not have tails.
Comets develop tails near the Sun.
A comet develops a coma and tail near the Sun.
A comet’s tail contains dust and ionised material.
A comet’s tail points away from the Sun.
Radiation pressure and solar wind direct a comet’s tail away from the Sun.
Halley’s Comet is a short-period comet.
Halley’s Comet has a period of about 76 years.
Halley’s Comet is next expected in 2061.
Hale-Bopp has a period of 2,534 years.
Shoemaker–Levy 9 collided with Jupiter in July 1994.
A meteoroid is a small rocky or metallic body in space.
A meteor is a bright streak produced when a meteoroid enters the atmosphere and heats up.
A meteor is popularly called a shooting star.
A meteorite is a meteoroid that survives and reaches the surface.
Atmospheric friction and heating cause a meteor to glow.
Kepler formulated the three laws of planetary motion.
Newton formulated the laws of gravity.
Johann Galle is associated with Neptune.

Earth has two primary motions: rotation and revolution.
Rotation means that Earth spins on its own axis.
Earth’s rotation causes day and night.
Earth’s rotation produces the Coriolis effect.
Earth’s rotation produces a centrifugal effect.
Revolution means that Earth moves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
Earth’s revolution causes seasons along with axial tilt.
Earth’s axis is an imaginary line joining the North and South Poles.
Earth rotates from west to east.
Earth appears to rotate counter-clockwise when viewed from the North Pole.
Earth completes one rotation in 24 hours.
Earth’s angular speed is 15° per hour.
A longitude difference of 1° corresponds to 4 minutes of time.
A longitude difference of 15° corresponds to 1 hour of time.
The main result of Earth’s rotation is day and night.
Earth’s rotation causes the Coriolis force and centrifugal effect.
Earth’s linear rotational speed is maximum at the Equator.
Earth’s linear rotational speed is zero at the Poles.
Day is experienced by the part of Earth facing the Sun.
Night is experienced by the part of Earth turned away from the Sun.
The circle of illumination divides the illuminated and dark portions of Earth.
Earth’s rotation on its axis causes day and night.
Earth’s revolution does not cause day and night.
Axial tilt alone does not cause day and night.
Earth completes a full rotation of 360° in 24 hours.
Local time advances when moving eastward.
Local time retards when moving westward.
A 180° longitude difference corresponds to 12 hours.
There are 24 theoretical world time zones, each covering 15°.
The Coriolis effect is caused by Earth’s rotation.
The Coriolis effect is the apparent deflection of moving objects or air.
Moving objects are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Moving objects are deflected to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Coriolis effect is zero or absent at the Equator.
The Coriolis effect is maximum at the Poles.
The Coriolis effect increases with latitude and velocity.
The Coriolis effect applies to winds, ocean currents, and cyclones.
The centrifugal effect is caused by Earth’s rotation.
The centrifugal effect is maximum at the Equator.
The centrifugal effect is minimum or zero at the Poles.
The centrifugal effect causes equatorial bulging and polar flattening.
Weight is minimum at the Equator.
Weight is maximum at the Poles.
Earth’s axis is an imaginary line through the North and South Poles.
Earth’s axial inclination is 23.5° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane.
Earth’s axis makes an angle of 66.5° with the orbital plane.
Earth’s axis remains approximately parallel during revolution.
Earth’s axial inclination is a major factor in seasons.
Earth’s revolution is its movement around the Sun.
Earth follows an elliptical orbit around the Sun.
Earth’s revolution period is also given as 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 9.51 seconds.
Earth’s average orbital speed is 29.78 km/s.
The major result of Earth’s revolution is the annual cycle.
Earth’s revolution produces seasons with axial tilt.
Earth’s axis maintains approximate parallelism during revolution.
Revolution changes Earth’s position around the Sun.
Earth’s axial tilt of 23.5° changes the angle and duration of solar illumination.
Parallelism of Earth’s axis produces opposite seasons in the two hemispheres.
Earth’s revolution and axial tilt produce the seasonal cycle.
The Northern Hemisphere summer solstice occurs approximately on 21 June.
The Sun’s direct rays fall on the Tropic of Cancer at the June summer solstice.
The Tropic of Cancer is at 23.5°N latitude.
The June solstice produces summer and the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere.
The June solstice produces winter and the shortest day in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Northern Hemisphere winter solstice occurs approximately on 21 or 22 December.
The Sun’s direct rays fall on the Tropic of Capricorn at the December winter solstice.
The Tropic of Capricorn is at 23.5°S latitude.
The December solstice produces winter and the shortest day in the Northern Hemisphere.
The December solstice produces summer and the longest day in the Southern Hemisphere.
An equinox means approximately equal day and night.
An equinox occurs twice a year.
The March equinox occurs approximately on 20 or 21 March.
The September equinox occurs approximately on 22 or 23 September.
The direct rays of the Sun fall on the Equator during an equinox.
Day and night are approximately equal during an equinox.
Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere at the March equinox.
Autumn begins in the Southern Hemisphere at the March equinox.
Autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere at the September equinox.
Spring begins in the Southern Hemisphere at the September equinox.
The Sun is overhead at the Equator on 21 March.
21 March is spring in the Northern Hemisphere.
21 March is autumn in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer on 21 June.
21 June is summer in the Northern Hemisphere.
21 June is winter in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Sun is overhead at the Equator on 23 September.
23 September is autumn in the Northern Hemisphere.
23 September is spring in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn on 22 December.
22 December is winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
22 December is summer in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day and shortest night on 21 June.
The Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day and longest night on 21 June.
The Northern Hemisphere has its shortest day and longest night on 21 or 22 December.
The Southern Hemisphere has its longest day and shortest night on 21 or 22 December.
The Northern and Southern Hemispheres have approximately equal day and night at the equinoxes.
Day and night are approximately equal throughout the year at the Equator.
The North Pole has six months of continuous daylight.
The North Pole has six months of darkness.
The South Pole has the opposite daylight and darkness pattern to the North Pole.
The main reason for polar six-month day and night is axial inclination combined with revolution.
Areas beyond the Arctic Circle experience continuous daylight during Northern Hemisphere summer.
Areas beyond the Antarctic Circle experience continuous daylight during Southern Hemisphere summer.
Summer has a more direct solar angle than winter.
Winter has a more slanting solar angle than summer.
Summer has longer days than winter.
Winter has shorter days than summer.
Earth receives greater solar energy in summer.
Earth receives lower solar energy in winter.
Perihelion is the position in which Earth is nearest to the Sun.
Perihelion occurs in early January, approximately on 4 January.
Earth is approximately 147 million km from the Sun at perihelion.
Earth’s orbital speed is greater at perihelion.
Aphelion is the position in which Earth is farthest from the Sun.
Aphelion occurs in early July, approximately on 4 July.
Earth is approximately 152 million km from the Sun at aphelion.
Earth’s orbital speed is lower at aphelion.
Earth’s maximum speed at perihelion is explained by Kepler’s Second Law.
Earth’s minimum speed at aphelion is explained by Kepler’s Second Law.
A normal calendar year has 365 days.
The extra fraction in a year is one-fourth of a day.
The extra fraction accumulates to one day in four years.
The extra day in a leap year is 29 February.
The Tropic of Cancer is at 23.5°N latitude.
The Sun is overhead near the June solstice at the Tropic of Cancer.
The Tropic of Capricorn is at 23.5°S latitude.
The Sun is overhead near the December solstice at the Tropic of Capricorn.
The Sun is overhead near the equinoxes at the Equator.
The Arctic Circle is at 66.5°N latitude.
The Arctic Circle is associated with polar day and night effects.
The Antarctic Circle is at 66.5°S latitude.
The Antarctic Circle is associated with polar day and night effects.
Parallelism means that Earth’s axis maintains approximately the same orientation as Earth revolves.
Parallelism of Earth’s axis produces seasonal reversal between the hemispheres.
The correct statement is that there is parallelism of Earth’s axis.
The centrifugal force is maximum at the Equator.
Earth’s shape resulting from equatorial bulging and polar flattening is an oblate spheroid.
Rotation makes weight minimum at the Equator and maximum at the Poles.
The 180° meridian is associated with the International Date Line.
The date changes across the International Date Line.
Earth’s rotation axis has shifted slightly over time.
The length of day has changed by a very small measurable amount.
Ice-sheet melting redistributes mass and water toward lower latitudes.
Redistribution of mass and water toward lower latitudes can influence Earth’s rotation and axis.
Solar flares and coronal mass ejections affect the upper atmosphere.
Solar flares and coronal mass ejections were not the primary explanation in the relevant question.
Rotation is movement on Earth’s axis.
Revolution is movement around the Sun.
Rotation has a period of 24 hours.
Revolution has a period of 365.25 days.
Rotation’s main result is day and night.
Revolution’s main result is a year.
Rotation has an indirect seasonal role.
Revolution has a direct seasonal role when combined with axial tilt.
Rotation has a role in the Coriolis effect.
Revolution has no primary role in the Coriolis effect.
Rotation has a role in the centrifugal effect.
Revolution does not produce time zones.
Rotation is not the direct cause of solstices and equinoxes.
Revolution causes solstices and equinoxes along with axial tilt.
Rotation does not cause perihelion and aphelion.
Revolution is associated with perihelion and aphelion.
Earth’s average orbital speed is 29.78 km/s.

Seasons occur because Earth revolves around the Sun and has an axial tilt of 23½°.

Earth’s axis is inclined 66½° to its orbital plane.
The main consequence of Earth’s revolution and axial tilt is a changing angle of insolation during the year.
Earth’s rotation causes day and night, not seasons.
Earth’s revolution alone is not sufficient to cause seasons.
Earth’s revolution needs axial tilt to produce seasons.
Distance from the Sun has only a minor or slight role in producing seasons.
The seasons in opposite hemispheres are opposite.
Rotation on its axis causes day and night.

Axial tilt combined with revolution causes changing day length.
Axial tilt combined with revolution causes solstices and equinoxes.

Earth’s position relative to the Sun changes during revolution.
Earth’s axial tilt remains approximately parallel during revolution.
The hemispheres alternately tilt toward and away from the Sun.
The angle of solar rays changes during the year.
The angle of insolation changes during the year.
The length of day changes during the year.
One hemisphere receives longer illumination at a time.

Winter solar rays are more oblique.

Winter solar energy has lower concentration.

The December solstice is the summer solstice for the Southern Hemisphere.

At an equinox, the Sun is overhead at the Equator.
Seasonal contrast is maximum at a solstice.
An equinox is a transition point between seasons.
Day and night are not equal at a solstice.
Day and night are approximately equal at an equinox.
The June solstice is associated with the Tropic of Cancer.
The December solstice is associated with the Tropic of Capricorn.
The equinoxes occur in March and September.

On 21 June, the Sun starts moving southward after being overhead at the Tropic of Cancer.

From 21 March to 21 June, Southern Hemisphere days progressively shorten.

The Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day on 21 June.

The Southern Hemisphere’s longest day occurs in the second half of December.
The Equator has approximately 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night throughout the year.
Seasonal variation in day length is very small at the Equator.
The Sun is overhead at the Equator during an equinox.
The Equator has no distinct winter or summer.

Polar night lasts approximately six months.

The vertical Sun is at the Equator on 21 March.

The vertical Sun is at the Tropic of Capricorn on 21 or 22 December.

More oblique or slanting solar rays spread energy over a larger area and produce lower heating.
The summer hemisphere receives more direct rays and longer days.
The winter hemisphere receives more oblique rays and shorter days.
A higher Sun in the sky produces a smaller shadow.
A lower Sun in the sky produces a longer shadow.
A vertically overhead Sun produces no shadow.

Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere.
December is winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
December is summer in the Southern Hemisphere.

Aphelion is the position of maximum Earth–Sun distance.
Earth’s orbital speed is faster at perihelion.
Earth’s orbital speed is slower at aphelion.
Perihelion occurs during the Northern Hemisphere’s winter period.

The retreating monsoon occurs from October to November.

Monsoonal climate has wet and dry seasons.

Seasonal temperature depends on insolation and day length.

S-waves stop in the outer core.

Seismic waves travel through different materials.
Seismic-wave velocity changes reveal differences in materials.
Seismic waves undergo reflection and refraction.

Temperature includes daily and annual ranges.
Temperature is controlled by latitude and altitude.
Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by air.

Humidity is the water vapour present in the atmosphere.
Cloudiness consists of condensed water or ice particles in the atmosphere.
Precipitation is water falling from the atmosphere.
Precipitation includes rain, snow, sleet and hail.
Sunshine or insolation is incoming solar energy.
Temperature range is the difference between maximum and minimum temperature.
Temperature generally decreases from the equator toward the poles.
Latitude affects temperature through the solar angle.
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude.
The Himalayas are cooler despite having a lower latitude.
Cloud cover modifies heating and cooling.
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature.
Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.
Cold ocean currents lower coastal temperatures.
Relief alters temperature and air movement.
Mountain slopes and aspects affect temperature.
Increasing temperature causes air to expand.
Expansion of air decreases air density.
Decreased air density produces low pressure.
Decreasing temperature causes air to contract.
Contraction of air increases air density.
Increased air density produces high pressure.

Seasonal heating causes seasonal wind reversal.

Cold air can hold less water vapour.

Clouds form through condensation around nuclei at altitude.

Temperate regions are typical locations for cyclonic or frontal precipitation.

Relief-induced precipitation differs between windward and leeward locations.
Cloudy conditions reduce incoming solar radiation during the day.
Cloudy conditions produce cooler daytime temperatures.
Cloudy conditions reduce terrestrial heat loss at night.
Clear skies allow greater solar heating during the day.
Clear skies cause greater terrestrial cooling at night.
The equator receives more direct rays.
More direct rays at the equator produce greater heating.
Oblique rays at the poles produce lower heating.
Annual temperature range is generally greater toward higher latitudes.
Lower temperature at higher altitude produces a cooler climate.
Lower atmospheric pressure occurs at higher altitude.
Mountain relief modifies rainfall and wind.
The sea heats and cools slowly.
Coastal regions have a smaller annual temperature range.
Interior regions have a larger annual temperature range.
Coastal regions have an equable climate.
Interior regions have a continental climate.
Summer heating produces low pressure over heated land.
A pressure gradient draws moisture-bearing winds.
The ITCZ shifts northward during summer.
The northward shift of the ITCZ helps monsoon circulation.
Winter cooling reverses the pressure pattern.
Winter cooling causes seasonal pressure reversal.
Seasonal pressure reversal causes seasonal wind reversal.
Mountains block or redirect air masses.
The Himalayas block cold continental winds.
The Western Ghats produce a strong rainfall contrast across their slopes.
Warm currents warm adjoining coastal air.
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates.

The Subtropical Westerly Jet is connected with winter weather.

An air mass is a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity.
An air mass forms over a source region with uniform surface properties.
A source region may be land or ocean.
Air masses are classified on the basis of the temperature and moisture content of their source regions.
An air mass travels away from its source region and gets modified.
Air masses control temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation.
Air masses from tropical oceans are warm and moist.
Tropical-ocean air masses are designated mT, meaning maritime Tropical.
Air masses from tropical land areas are warm and dry.
Tropical-land air masses are designated cT, meaning continental Tropical.
Air masses from polar oceans are cold and moist.
Polar-ocean air masses are designated mP, meaning maritime Polar.
Air masses from polar land areas are cold and dry.
Polar-land air masses are designated cP, meaning continental Polar.
Arctic and Antarctic air masses are extremely cold and dry.
Arctic and Antarctic air masses are designated cA or cAA.
An air mass loses its original characteristics as it moves away from its source region.
An air mass becomes warmer and more unstable when it passes over a warm surface.
An air mass becomes cooler and more stable when it passes over a cold surface.
An air mass gains moisture when it passes over an ocean.
An air mass loses moisture and becomes drier when it passes over land.
Vertical mixing alters the temperature and humidity profile of an air mass.
A front is a boundary zone between two contrasting air masses.
A front forms when two air masses with different temperatures and humidity meet.
Lighter, warmer air is forced to rise over denser, colder air at a front.
The uplift of warm air produces cooling.
A warm front forms when warm air advances over cold air.
A warm front produces gradual uplift.
A warm front produces widespread light to moderate rain.
A cold front forms when cold air undercuts warm air.
A cold front produces steep uplift.
A cold front produces intense short-duration rain and thunderstorms.
An occluded front forms when a cold front overtakes a warm front.
An occluded front produces complex weather.
An occluded front often produces prolonged precipitation.
A stationary front occurs when neither air mass advances.
A stationary front produces prolonged cloudy and rainy conditions.
Uplift at a front forces air to rise.
Adiabatic cooling causes temperature to fall to the dew point.
Condensation begins when air cools to the dew point.
Condensation changes water vapour into liquid or ice particles.
Precipitation occurs when droplets grow and fall.
Precipitation may produce rain, snow or sleet.
The final impact of the uplift chain includes changes in wind, temperature, humidity and pressure.
The final impact of the uplift chain includes changes in weather systems and climatic patterns.
A new air mass can cause a sudden rise or fall in temperature.
Frontal uplift produces cyclonic or frontal rainfall.
Seasonal shifts in air masses produce seasonal climatic changes.
Monsoon winds are an example of seasonal shifts in air masses.
Air masses and fronts can produce cold waves.
Air masses and fronts can produce heat waves.
Air masses and fronts can produce thunderstorms.
Air masses and fronts can produce blizzards.
Persistent air-mass influence creates characteristic regional climates.
Maritime and continental climates are examples of characteristic regional climates.

A tropical cyclone is a low-pressure system over warm tropical oceans.
A temperate or extratropical cyclone is a mid-latitude cyclone associated with air-mass interaction.
A temperate or extratropical cyclone is large-scale.
An anticyclone has a high-pressure centre.

A thunderstorm is local in scale.

Spiral rainbands are curved cloud bands that produce rain and wind.
The centre of a tropical cyclone is the region of lowest pressure.
Tropical cyclones rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.

Air moves outward in an anticyclone.
Cyclonic weather is cloudier and stormier.

Anticyclones rotate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.
Cyclones rotate clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

Temperate or extratropical cyclones occur mainly in the mid-latitudes, approximately 35°–65° in both hemispheres.

The key mechanism of temperate or extratropical cyclones is the interaction of contrasting air masses.
Fronts are associated with temperate or extratropical cyclones.

A Western Disturbance is an extratropical or cyclonic disturbance.
A Western Disturbance originates in the Mediterranean region.
Westerlies and the Subtropical Westerly Jet steer Western Disturbances.
Western Disturbances occur mainly in winter.
Northwestern India is the main region affected by Western Disturbances.
Western Disturbances bring snowfall to mountains.
Western Disturbance rainfall is agriculturally important for Rabi crops.

The Gulf of Mexico supplies warm, moisture-rich air to the tornado-prone USA.
Cold, drier continental air contributes to tornado formation in the tornado-prone USA.
Atmospheric instability contributes to tornado formation in the tornado-prone USA.

Severe thunderstorms or supercells create tornado potential.
